title: Ayurveda Expert Shares 21-Day Routine for Glowing Skin, Centered on Gut Health
excerpt: Dr Hansa Yogendra, director of The Yoga Institute in Mumbai, has laid out a three-week regimen built around a simple ginger-cardamom morning drink, gentle Ayurvedic skincare rituals and diet — arguing that radiant skin starts with a healthy gut.
body:
• Dr Hansa Yogendra, director of The Yoga Institute in Mumbai, has outlined a 21-day routine for naturally glowing skin, organized into three weekly phases: cleansing, gentle exfoliation and deep nourishment.
  • Week one centers on a "Cleanse and Calm" morning drink — ginger, green cardamom and rose petals simmered in water — taken warm on an empty stomach.
  • The plan pairs kitchen-ingredient rituals, including a natural ubtan, a sandalwood-and-lotus mask and an aloe vera mask, with protein- and vitamin C-rich foods to support collagen, plus face yoga and breathwork.
  • The underlying premise is Ayurvedic: the skin reflects inner health, so digestion, sleep, hydration and stress management are treated as skincare inputs.

Ayurveda expert Dr Hansa Yogendra, director of The Yoga Institute in Mumbai, has shared a structured 21-day plan for naturally glowing skin in a recent video, putting a simple homemade morning drink and a healthy gut at the center of the routine. The regimen, divided into three weekly phases, blends dietary guidance with Ayurvedic skincare rituals made from everyday kitchen ingredients.

According to Dr Yogendra, radiant skin is not produced by creams alone. In the tradition of Yoga and Ayurveda, the skin also reflects digestion, nourishment, stress, sleep and everyday lifestyle — so the plan treats what happens inside the body as seriously as what goes on the face.

The plan, week by week

Week one focuses on cleansing and calming the skin. Each morning begins with a skin-glow infusion taken on an empty stomach, alongside a gentle sandalwood-and-lotus face mask. Week two moves to gentle exfoliation with a natural ubtan — the traditional Ayurvedic paste — plus a second skin-glow drink. Week three is about deep nourishment from within: a nourishing aloe vera face mask, foods rich in protein and vitamin C to support collagen formation, and practices such as face yoga, Kapalarandhra Dhauti and Kapalabhati breathing.

"Week one centers on a "Cleanse and Calm" morning drink — ginger, green cardamom and rose petals simmered in water — taken warm on an empty stomach."

Throughout the three weeks, the routine also calls for mindful eating, adequate hydration and stress management — a holistic approach rather than a single-product fix.

The 'Cleanse and Calm' morning drink

The drink Dr Yogendra recommends is deliberately simple. The ingredients, according to the recipe shared with the video, are one cup of water, one teaspoon of crushed ginger, two green cardamom pods lightly crushed, and a few rose petals. The method: add everything to a saucepan, bring to a boil, simmer for about five minutes, strain and drink warm.

She suggests drinking it every morning on an empty stomach, and emphasizes that a healthy gut is essential for radiant skin — the herbal drink, she says, may help cleanse the body and support gut health naturally.

Why inner health comes first

The ingredient list reads like a pantry tour of Ayurvedic skincare: rose water, besan (gram flour), ginger, mint leaves, cardamom, turmeric, cinnamon and aloe vera gel. These are chosen not for cosmetic effect alone but for their traditional roles — supporting digestion, reducing inflammation and hydrating the body from within, which gradually improves skin brightness and moisture, according to the video.

The approach also builds in caution: viewers are advised to patch-test new skincare ingredients, especially if they have sensitive or acne-prone skin.

A routine built for Indian kitchens

For the Indian diaspora, the plan may feel less like a new regimen and more like a return to familiar ground. Ginger, cardamom, turmeric, besan and rose water are staples in most diaspora kitchens, which makes the routine inexpensive and easy to follow without specialist products. The Yoga Institute, founded in Mumbai in 1918, is among the world's oldest organized yoga centers, and its routines carry the weight of that institutional lineage for viewers in India and abroad.

The timing also aligns with a broader clean-beauty movement that has made "skin from within" a mainstream idea — though Ayurveda has treated gut health, sleep and stress as skincare fundamentals for centuries.

What's next

Dr Yogendra's underlying message is consistency over quick fixes: natural routines take time, and the 21-day window is a starting commitment rather than a deadline. Those trying the plan should keep expectations realistic, patch-test topical ingredients and remember that persistent skin concerns deserve professional medical advice. The full routine is available as a video on The Yoga Institute's official channel.
